claim: MELK over-expression is associated with aggressive disease in multiple cancer types.
source: MELK over-expression is associated with aggressive disease, and MELK has been implicated in numerous cancer-related processes, including chemotherapy resistance, stem cell renewal, and tumor growth.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature establishing this association.

claim: MELK has been implicated in chemotherapy resistance, stem cell renewal, and tumor growth.
source: MELK over-expression is associated with aggressive disease, and MELK has been implicated in numerous cancer-related processes, including chemotherapy resistance, stem cell renewal, and tumor growth.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Triple-negative breast cancer cell lines harboring CRISPR/Cas9-induced null mutations in MELK proliferate at wild-type levels in vitro.
source: Previously, we established that triple-negative breast cancer cell lines harboring CRISPR/Cas9-induced null mutations in MELK proliferate at wild-type levels in vitro (Lin et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to the authors' previous work.

claim: Cells lacking MELK exhibit wild-type growth in vitro across cancer types.
source: Here, we generate several additional knockout clones of MELK and demonstrate that across cancer types, cells lacking MELK exhibit wild-type growth in vitro, under environmental stress, in the presence of cytotoxic chemotherapies, and in vivo.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Cells lacking MELK exhibit wild-type growth under environmental stress.
source: Here, we generate several additional knockout clones of MELK and demonstrate that across cancer types, cells lacking MELK exhibit wild-type growth in vitro, under environmental stress, in the presence of cytotoxic chemotherapies, and in vivo.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Cells lacking MELK exhibit wild-type growth in the presence of cytotoxic chemotherapies.
source: Here, we generate several additional knockout clones of MELK and demonstrate that across cancer types, cells lacking MELK exhibit wild-type growth in vitro, under environmental stress, in the presence of cytotoxic chemotherapies, and in vivo.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Cells lacking MELK exhibit wild-type growth in vivo.
source: Here, we generate several additional knockout clones of MELK and demonstrate that across cancer types, cells lacking MELK exhibit wild-type growth in vitro, under environmental stress, in the presence of cytotoxic chemotherapies, and in vivo.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Acute inhibition of MELK results in no specific anti-proliferative phenotype.
source: By combining our MELK-knockout clones with a recently described, highly specific MELK inhibitor, we further demonstrate that the acute inhibition of MELK results in no specific anti-proliferative phenotype.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data using a MELK inhibitor combined with knockout clones.

claim: MELK expression is a correlate of tumor mitotic activity.
source: Analysis of gene expression data from cohorts of cancer patients identifies MELK expression as a correlate of tumor mitotic activity, explaining its association with poor clinical prognosis.
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of gene expression data from patient cohorts.

claim: MELK expression's correlation with tumor mitotic activity explains its association with poor clinical prognosis.
source: Analysis of gene expression data from cohorts of cancer patients identifies MELK expression as a correlate of tumor mitotic activity, explaining its association with poor clinical prognosis.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the correlation analysis presented.

claim: MELK has been identified as a promising therapeutic target in multiple cancer types.
source: The Maternal Embryonic Leucine Zipper Kinase (MELK) has been identified as a promising therapeutic target in multiple cancer types.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: MELK has been implicated as a cancer dependency and putative drug target in melanoma, colorectal cancer, and triple-negative breast cancer.
source: The Maternal Embryonic Leucine Zipper Kinase (MELK) has been implicated as a cancer dependency and putative drug target in multiple cancer types, including melanoma, colorectal cancer, and triple-negative breast cancer (Chung et al., 2012; Speers et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2014; Ganguly et al., 2014a; Ganguly et al., 2014b; Janostiak et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: High expression of MELK is associated with poor patient prognosis in multiple cancer types.
source: MELK is over-expressed in these cancers, and high expression of MELK is associated with poor patient prognosis (Wang et al., 2014; Pickard et al., 2009; Phillips et al., 2006; Ryu et al., 2007; Gray et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Knockdown of MELK using RNA interference has been reported to block cancer cell proliferation and trigger cell cycle arrest or mitotic catastrophe.
source: Moreover, knockdown of MELK using RNA interference (RNAi) has been reported to block cancer cell proliferation and trigger cell cycle arrest or mitotic catastrophe (Speers et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2014; Gray et al., 2005; Kuner et al., 2013; Lin et al., 2007; Beke et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Several companies have developed small-molecule MELK inhibitors.
source: On the basis of these pre-clinical results, several companies have developed small-molecule MELK inhibitors, and one MELK inhibitor (OTS167) is currently being tested in multiple clinical trials (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to ClinicalTrials.gov.

claim: The MELK inhibitor OTS167 is currently being tested in multiple clinical trials.
source: On the basis of these pre-clinical results, several companies have developed small-molecule MELK inhibitors, and one MELK inhibitor (OTS167) is currently being tested in multiple clinical trials (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to ClinicalTrials.gov.

claim: The MELK inhibitor OTS167 remained effective against MELK-mutant cells.
source: Additionally, we demonstrated that the MELK inhibitor OTS167 remained effective against MELK-mutant cells, suggesting that OTS167 kills cells through an off-target mechanism.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to the authors' previous work.

claim: OTS167 kills cells through an off-target mechanism.
source: Additionally, we demonstrated that the MELK inhibitor OTS167 remained effective against MELK-mutant cells, suggesting that OTS167 kills cells through an off-target mechanism.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the observation that OTS167 affects MELK-mutant cells.

claim: The shRNA vectors commonly used to study MELK kill cells in a MELK-independent manner.
source: These results have been replicated by an independent group, who further demonstrated that the shRNA vectors commonly used to study MELK also kill cells in a MELK-independent manner (Huang et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to another group's work.

claim: MELK expression remains one of the strongest predictors of patient mortality in diverse cancer types.
source: Despite the conflicting in vitro data, MELK expression remains one of the strongest predictors of patient mortality in diverse cancer types (Smith and Sheltzer, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation.

claim: MELK has been implicated in cancer stem cell maintenance, chemotherapy resistance, anchorage-independent growth, and reactive oxygen species (ROS)-signaling.
source: Additionally, MELK has been implicated in several other cancer-related processes, including cancer stem cell maintenance, chemotherapy resistance, anchorage-independent growth, and reactive oxygen species (ROS)-signaling (Wang et al., 2014; Ganguly et al., 2014a; Beke et al., 2015; Kim et al., 2015; Seong et al., 2016; Choi et al., 2011; Gu et al., 2013; Hebbard et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The over-expression of MELK has been reported to transform cells.
source: Moreover, the over-expression of MELK has been reported to transform cells, suggesting that in addition to MELK's putative role as a cancer dependency, it may also function as a driver oncogene (Wang et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: MELK may function as a driver oncogene.
source: Moreover, the over-expression of MELK has been reported to transform cells, suggesting that in addition to MELK's putative role as a cancer dependency, it may also function as a driver oncogene (Wang et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on inference from reported transformation ability.

claim: CRISPR/Cas9 mutagenesis is prone to limitations including selection for secondary mutations during clonal expansion.
source: While RNA interference is susceptible to off-target interactions that confound experimental interpretation (Jackson et al., 2003, 2006), CRISPR/Cas9 mutagenesis is also prone to several important limitations. In particular, clonal cell lines harboring Cas9-induced modifications must be expanded from a single cell with a mutation of interest to several million cells. This intense pressure may select for secondary mutations that blunt any anti-proliferative consequences of the original mutation (Iwasa et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature on CRISPR limitations.

claim: The immediate inhibition of a target with a small-molecule drug may induce a more severe phenotype than observed in a CRISPR-modified cell line subjected to evolutionary pressure.
source: In a therapeutic context, the immediate inhibition of a particular target achieved with a small-molecule drug may induce a more severe phenotype than observed in a CRISPR-modified cell line subjected to evolutionary pressure over the course of days or weeks.
evidence: This claim is based on logical inference about differences between genetic and pharmacological approaches.

claim: The over-expression of MELK was sufficient to induce anchorage-independent growth in Rat1 fibroblasts expressing dominant-negative p53 and MCF10A cells.
source: It has previously been reported that the over-expression of MELK was sufficient to induce anchorage-independent growth in several cell lines, including Rat1 fibroblasts expressing dominant-negative p53 (p53dd) and the human mammary epithelial cell line MCF10A (Wang et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Full-length mouse or human MELK was over-expressed in all six cell lines generated relative to vector-transduced control cell lines.
source: Western blot analysis confirmed that full-length mouse or human MELK was over-expressed in all six cell lines that we generated relative to the level of MELK in vector-transduced control cell lines (Figure 1A,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1A and 1D.

claim: Both ectopic and endogenous MELK were stabilized and phosphorylated in mitotic cells.
source: Consistent with previous reports (Gray et al., 2005; Badouel et al., 2010), we found that both ectopic and endogenous MELK were stabilized and phosphorylated in mitotic cells, suggesting that the transgenic MELK was functional (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and citations to prior literature.

claim: The transgenic MELK was functional.
source: Consistent with previous reports (Gray et al., 2005; Badouel et al., 2010), we found that both ectopic and endogenous MELK were stabilized and phosphorylated in mitotic cells, suggesting that the transgenic MELK was functional (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that transgenic MELK behaves like endogenous MELK in mitotic cells.

claim: The over-expression of driver oncogenes allows immortalized but non-transformed cell lines to form colonies when grown in soft agar.
source: The over-expression of driver oncogenes allows immortalized but non-transformed cell lines to form colonies when grown in soft agar, a phenotype that is tightly linked with in vivo tumorigenicity (Shin et al., 1975; Colburn et al., 1978; Cifone and Fidler, 1980).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature establishing this relationship.

claim: Anchorage-independent growth is tightly linked with in vivo tumorigenicity.
source: The over-expression of driver oncogenes allows immortalized but non-transformed cell lines to form colonies when grown in soft agar, a phenotype that is tightly linked with in vivo tumorigenicity (Shin et al., 1975; Colburn et al., 1978; Cifone and Fidler, 1980).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Cells transduced with H-RasG12V or EGFRL858R formed numerous colonies in soft agar.
source: As expected, cells that had been transduced with an empty vector exhibited minimal anchorage-independent growth, while cells transduced with H-RasG12V or EGFRL858R formed numerous colonies (Figure 1B–C and E–F).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1B-C and E-F.

claim: Cells transduced with an empty vector exhibited minimal anchorage-independent growth.
source: As expected, cells that had been transduced with an empty vector exhibited minimal anchorage-independent growth, while cells transduced with H-RasG12V or EGFRL858R formed numerous colonies (Figure 1B–C and E–F).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1B-C and E-F.

claim: The over-expression of MELK fails to induce anchorage-independent growth in any of the six cell lines tested.
source: However, in multiple independent experiments, we failed to detect an increase in anchorage-independent growth in any of the six cell lines over-expressing either mouse or human MELK.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from soft agar assays.

claim: Under the conditions tested, the over-expression of MELK fails to transform cells.
source: We conclude that, under the conditions tested, the over-expression of MELK fails to transform cells.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the soft agar assay data presented.

claim: MELK was not required for cell division in Cal51 and MDA-MB-231 triple-negative breast cancer cell lines.
source: We previously showed that MELK was not required for cell division in two triple-negative breast cancer cell lines, Cal51 and MDA-MB-231 (Lin et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to the authors' previous work.

claim: MELK has been reported to support growth in colorectal cancer and melanoma.
source: However, MELK has been reported to support growth in several other cancer types, including colorectal cancer and melanoma (Ganguly et al., 2014b; Janostiak et al., 2017; Gray et al., 2005; Choi et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: MELK-knockout melanoma and colorectal cancer clones grew at wild-type levels in vitro.
source: MELK-KO melanoma and colorectal cancer clones grew at wild-type levels in vitro, demonstrating that MELK is dispensable for proliferation in these cancer types as well (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by proliferation data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: MELK is dispensable for proliferation in melanoma and colorectal cancer.
source: MELK-KO melanoma and colorectal cancer clones grew at wild-type levels in vitro, demonstrating that MELK is dispensable for proliferation in these cancer types as well (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This conclusion is based on the proliferation data presented.

claim: MELK-KO and Rosa26 clones were equally sensitive to OTS167.
source: Consistent with these observations, MELK-KO and Rosa26 clones were equally sensitive to OTS167, verifying that this drug kills cells via an off-target effect across cancer types (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by dose-response data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: OTS167 kills cells via an off-target effect across cancer types.
source: Consistent with these observations, MELK-KO and Rosa26 clones were equally sensitive to OTS167, verifying that this drug kills cells via an off-target effect across cancer types (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This conclusion is inferred from the observation that MELK-KO cells are equally sensitive to OTS167.

claim: Many genes that are non-essential for cell division in vitro may still play crucial roles in cancer by supporting other processes.
source: Many genes that are non-essential for cell division in vitro may still play crucial roles in cancer by supporting other processes, including stem-cell renewal, resistance to anoikis, and angiogenesis (Rotem et al., 2015; Zhong et al., 2011; Miller et al., 2017; Cidado et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The loss of MELK failed to impair colony growth relative to control Rosa26 cell lines.
source: Crystal violet staining of these plates revealed that the loss of MELK failed to impair colony growth relative to the control Rosa26 cell lines (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by crystal violet staining data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: One MELK-KO clone (MDA-MB-231 c1) grew consistently better than either control clone in the colony growth assay.
source: In fact, one MELK-KO clone (MDA-MB-231 c1) grew consistently better than either control clone in this assay.
evidence: This claim is supported by data from the colony growth assay.

claim: Significant variation in proliferative capacity has been described among independent clones of the MDA-MB-231 cell line.
source: Significant variation in proliferative capacity has previously been described among independent clones of the MDA-MB-231 cell line (Khan et al., 2017) and may arise due to heterogeneity in the parental population or secondary mutations acquired during cell line derivation.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Variation in proliferative capacity may arise due to heterogeneity in the parental population or secondary mutations acquired during cell line derivation.
source: Significant variation in proliferative capacity has previously been described among independent clones of the MDA-MB-231 cell line (Khan et al., 2017) and may arise due to heterogeneity in the parental population or secondary mutations acquired during cell line derivation.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for observed variation.

claim: No significant difference in anchorage-independent growth was observed between MELK-KO cells and Rosa26 cells in every cell line tested.
source: However, we observed no significant difference in anchorage-independent growth between MELK-KO cells and Rosa26 cells in every cell line tested (Figure 2B–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by soft agar assay data shown in Figure 2B-C.

claim: MELK has been implicated in the maintenance of breast cancer stem cells.
source: MELK has previously been implicated in the maintenance of breast cancer stem cells (Ganguly et al., 2014a; Gu et al., 2013; Kig et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Mammosphere formation is a phenotype tightly linked with breast cancer stem cell activity.
source: We therefore tested whether loss of MELK impairs mammosphere formation, a phenotype tightly linked with breast cancer stem cell activity (Grimshaw et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: All MELK-KO clones were capable of forming mammospheres.
source: While we observed inter-clonal variability in mammosphere growth, all MELK-KO clones were capable of forming mammospheres, and two MELK-KO clones exhibited consistently greater mammosphere formation than their wild-type controls (Figure 2D–E).
evidence: This claim is supported by mammosphere assay data shown in Figure 2D-E.

claim: Two MELK-KO clones exhibited consistently greater mammosphere formation than their wild-type controls.
source: While we observed inter-clonal variability in mammosphere growth, all MELK-KO clones were capable of forming mammospheres, and two MELK-KO clones exhibited consistently greater mammosphere formation than their wild-type controls (Figure 2D–E).
evidence: This claim is supported by mammosphere assay data shown in Figure 2D-E.

claim: MELK is dispensable for growth as a mammosphere.
source: We conclude that MELK is dispensable for growth as a mammosphere.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the mammosphere assay data.

claim: 23 of 34 injections with MELK-KO cells and 24 of 34 injections with Rosa26 cells resulted in detectable tumor formation.
source: Across all clones tested, 23 of 34 injections with MELK-KO cells and 24 of 34 injections with Rosa26 cells resulted in detectable tumor formation, and no significant growth defect was observed in any MELK-KO clone (Figure 2F–G).
evidence: This claim is supported by xenograft data shown in Figure 2F-G.

claim: No significant growth defect was observed in any MELK-KO clone in xenograft assays.
source: Across all clones tested, 23 of 34 injections with MELK-KO cells and 24 of 34 injections with Rosa26 cells resulted in detectable tumor formation, and no significant growth defect was observed in any MELK-KO clone (Figure 2F–G).
evidence: This claim is supported by xenograft data shown in Figure 2F-G.

claim: MDA-MB-231 MELK-KO c1 clone exhibited superior growth in xenograft assays.
source: Consistent with our previous assays, we observed superior growth in the MDA-MB-231 MELK-KO c1 clone, while MDA-MB-231 MELK-KO c2 and Rosa26 c2 grew slowly but at equivalent rates (Figure 2G).
evidence: This claim is supported by xenograft data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: MDA-MB-231 is reported to grow aggressively in vivo.
source: The slow growth of MDA-MB-231 Rosa26 c1, MELK-KO c2, and Rosa26 c2 was unexpected, as MDA-MB-231 is reported to grow aggressively in vivo (Price et al., 1990).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Cells in the parental MDA-MB-231 population exhibit different abilities to form tumors.
source: We hypothesized that the poor growth of many of our MDA-MB-231 clones could reflect the fact that cells in the parental population exhibit different abilities to form tumors, and by chance, we isolated several clones with limited tumor-initiating capacity (Fillmore and Kuperwasser, 2008; Charafe-Jauffret et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by citations to prior literature on tumor heterogeneity.

claim: Transduction with MELK-targeting gRNAs ablated MELK protein expression in MDA-MB-231 populations.
source: Western blot analysis verified that transduction with the MELK-targeting gRNAs ablated MELK protein expression (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A.

claim: MELK-depleted MDA-MB-231 cell populations exhibited equivalent or superior tumor growth compared to control populations.
source: After injection into nude mice, these cell populations grew more rapidly than any clonal cell line, and the MELK-depleted cells exhibited equivalent or superior tumor growth compared to the control populations (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by xenograft data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B.

claim: MELK is dispensable for the proliferation of cancer cells in vitro and in vivo.
source: In total, these results demonstrate that MELK is dispensable for the proliferation of cancer cells in vitro and in vivo.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the comprehensive set of in vitro and in vivo assays presented.

claim: MELK has been reported to phosphorylate eukaryotic translation initiation factor 4B (eIF4B).
source: In particular, a recent publication reported that MELK phosphorylates eukaryotic translation initiation factor 4B (eIF4B), and this phosphorylation event promotes cell survival by increasing translation of the anti-apoptotic protein MCL1 (Wang et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: MELK phosphorylation of eIF4B promotes cell survival by increasing translation of MCL1.
source: In particular, a recent publication reported that MELK phosphorylates eukaryotic translation initiation factor 4B (eIF4B), and this phosphorylation event promotes cell survival by increasing translation of the anti-apoptotic protein MCL1 (Wang et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: MELK-knockout A375, Cal51 and MDA-MB-231 cells showed normal levels of eIF4B phosphorylation.
source: However, western blot analysis revealed normal levels of eIF4B phosphorylation in MELK-knockout A375, Cal51 and MDA-MB-231 cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A-C.

claim: MELK-KO cell lines continued to express MCL1.
source: Additionally, MELK-KO cell lines continued to express MCL1, the putative downstream target of eIF4B (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D–E).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D-E.

claim: MELK is not required for eIF4B phosphorylation or MCL1 translation.
source: We conclude that MELK is not required for eIF4B phosphorylation or MCL1 translation.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the western blot data showing normal eIF4B phosphorylation and MCL1 expression in MELK-KO cells.

claim: Developing tumors must survive in hypoxic and nutrient-poor conditions.
source: Developing tumors must survive in hypoxic and nutrient-poor conditions (Vaupel et al., 1989), and MELK has been implicated in glucose signaling and in the detection of ROS (Seong et al., 2016; Jung et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: MELK has been implicated in glucose signaling and in the detection of ROS.
source: Developing tumors must survive in hypoxic and nutrient-poor conditions (Vaupel et al., 1989), and MELK has been implicated in glucose signaling and in the detection of ROS (Seong et al., 2016; Jung et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: No difference in sensitivity to H2O2 was observed between MELK-KO and control Rosa26 clones.
source: To generate ROS stress, we cultured cells in varying concentrations of H2O2, but we observed no difference in sensitivity between MELK-KO and control Rosa26 clones (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by dose-response data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: MELK has been suggested to contribute to ROS signaling by phosphorylating ASK1.
source: MELK has been suggested to contribute to ROS signaling by phosphorylating ASK1 (Jung et al., 2008); however, this protein remained phosphorylated at normal levels in cells lacking MELK (Figure 3—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: ASK1 remained phosphorylated at normal levels in cells lacking MELK.
source: MELK has been suggested to contribute to ROS signaling by phosphorylating ASK1 (Jung et al., 2008); however, this protein remained phosphorylated at normal levels in cells lacking MELK (Figure 3—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1F.

claim: MELK-KO clones exhibited wild-type levels of growth when cultured under hypoxic, serum-deprived, or glucose-limited conditions.
source: MELK-KO clones also exhibited wild-type levels of growth when cultured under hypoxic, serum-deprived, or glucose-limited conditions (Figure 3B–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by crystal violet staining data shown in Figure 3B-D.

claim: MELK is dispensable for proliferation under common metabolic stresses.
source: We conclude that MELK is dispensable for proliferation under common metabolic stresses.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the stress assay data presented.

claim: Knocking down or inhibiting MELK sensitizes cells to DNA damage.
source: Indeed, it has been previously reported that knocking down or inhibiting MELK sensitizes cells to DNA damage (Beke et al., 2015; Kim et al., 2015; Choi et al., 2011; Kig et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The loss of MELK failed to sensitize cells to five common chemotherapies.
source: However, we found that the loss of MELK failed to sensitizes cells to five common chemotherapies (Figure 3E–I).
evidence: This claim is supported by dose-response data shown in Figure 3E-I.

claim: MELK is dispensable for cell survival under metabolic and cytotoxic stress.
source: In total, these results demonstrate that MELK is dispensable for cell survival under metabolic and cytotoxic stress.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the comprehensive stress and chemotherapy assay data.

claim: 1 µM HTH-01–091 triggered near-complete MELK degradation in Cal51, DLD1, and MDA-MB-231 cells.
source: We found that 1 µM HTH-01–091 triggered near-complete MELK degradation in Cal51, DLD1, and MDA-MB-231 cells (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The loss of MELK after HTH-01–091 treatment was not an indirect effect of cell cycle arrest.
source: The loss of MELK was not an indirect effect of cell cycle arrest, as these cells maintained high levels of the mitotic marker cyclin B.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that cyclin B levels remained high.

claim: Neither MELK-KO nor Rosa26 clones were affected by HTH-01–091 treatment in colony formation and anchorage-independent growth assays.
source: To test whether the acute inhibition of MELK affected clonogenicity or anchorage-independent growth, we grew MELK-KO and Rosa26 cells on plastic or in soft agar in the presence of DMSO or 1 µM HTH-01–091. Neither MELK-KO nor Rosa26 clones were affected by HTH-01–091 treatment, verifying that MELK is dispensable for colony formation and anchorage-independent growth in these cells (Figure 4B–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4B-C.

claim: MELK is dispensable for colony formation and anchorage-independent growth.
source: To test whether the acute inhibition of MELK affected clonogenicity or anchorage-independent growth, we grew MELK-KO and Rosa26 cells on plastic or in soft agar in the presence of DMSO or 1 µM HTH-01–091. Neither MELK-KO nor Rosa26 clones were affected by HTH-01–091 treatment, verifying that MELK is dispensable for colony formation and anchorage-independent growth in these cells (Figure 4B–C).
evidence: This conclusion is based on the HTH-01–091 treatment data.

claim: HTH-01–091 exhibited significant anti-proliferative effects only at concentrations above ~5 µM.
source: Indeed, a drug sensitivity assay revealed that HTH-01–091 exhibited significant anti-proliferative effects only at concentrations above ~5 µM (Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is supported by dose-response data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The toxicity of HTH-01–091 at high concentrations is likely a consequence of an off-target effect.
source: This toxicity is likely a consequence of an off-target effect, as these drug concentrations were found to affect Rosa26 and MELK-KO cells equivalently.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that both Rosa26 and MELK-KO cells are equally affected.

claim: HTH-01–091 treatment failed to sensitize Rosa26 clones to 5-fluorouracil or paclitaxel treatment.
source: Consistent with our previous results, HTH-01–091 treatment failed to sensitize the Rosa26 clones to 5-florouracil or paclitaxel treatment (Figure 4E).
evidence: This claim is supported by dose-response data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: MELK inhibition failed to affect eIF4B phosphorylation and MCL1 expression.
source: Finally, we assessed the effect of HTH-01–091 treatment on eIF4B phosphorylation and MCL1 expression, and found that MELK inhibition failed to affect either target (Figure 3—figure supplement 1G–H).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1G-H.

claim: The acute loss of MELK results in no significant defect in cell viability, proliferation, or drug resistance.
source: In total, these results demonstrate that the acute loss of MELK results in no significant defect in cell viability, proliferation, or drug resistance and suggest that our knockout clones have not acquired mutations that tolerize cells to the loss of MELK.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the comprehensive HTH-01–091 treatment data.

claim: The knockout clones have not acquired mutations that tolerize cells to the loss of MELK.
source: In total, these results demonstrate that the acute loss of MELK results in no significant defect in cell viability, proliferation, or drug resistance and suggest that our knockout clones have not acquired mutations that tolerize cells to the loss of MELK.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that acute MELK inhibition produces the same result as genetic knockout.

claim: MELK is up-regulated in many cancer types.
source: Yet, MELK is up-regulated in many cancer types (Gray et al., 2005), and high levels of MELK expression have been reported to confer a dismal clinical prognosis (Wang et al., 2014; Pickard et al., 2009; Phillips et al., 2006; Ryu et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: High levels of MELK expression have been reported to confer a dismal clinical prognosis.
source: Yet, MELK is up-regulated in many cancer types (Gray et al., 2005), and high levels of MELK expression have been reported to confer a dismal clinical prognosis (Wang et al., 2014; Pickard et al., 2009; Phillips et al., 2006; Ryu et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: MELK expression is cell cycle-regulated, peaking in mitosis.
source: We note that MELK expression is cell cycle-regulated, peaking in mitosis (Wang et al., 2014; Badouel et al., 2010), and gene signatures that capture mitotic activity have been found to be prognostic in multiple cancer types (Smith and Sheltzer, 2017; Venet et al., 2011; Gentles et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Gene signatures that capture mitotic activity have been found to be prognostic in multiple cancer types.
source: We note that MELK expression is cell cycle-regulated, peaking in mitosis (Wang et al., 2014; Badouel et al., 2010), and gene signatures that capture mitotic activity have been found to be prognostic in multiple cancer types (Smith and Sheltzer, 2017; Venet et al., 2011; Gentles et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: MELK expression may function as an indirect proxy for rapid cell division.
source: We therefore considered the possibility that, rather than functioning as an oncogene or a cancer dependency, MELK expression could report cell division within a tumor.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the cell cycle-regulated nature of MELK.

claim: In normal human tissue, MELK transcript expression was lowest in non-proliferative organs and highest in organs with on-going mitotic activity.
source: In normal human tissue, MELK transcript expression was the lowest in non-proliferative organs, including the heart and skeletal muscle, while MELK expression was the highest in organs with on-going mitotic activity, including the bone marrow and testes (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Across 32 tissue types, MELK levels were highly correlated with the expression of the proliferation marker MKI67 (R = 0.93).
source: Indeed, across 32 tissue types, MELK levels were highly correlated with the expression of the proliferation marker MKI67 (R = 0.93).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis of gene expression data.

claim: In human fibroblasts cultured until senescence, MELK expression decreased up to 11-fold between proliferating and arrested populations.
source: Similarly, in human fibroblasts cultured until senescence, MELK expression decreased up to 11-fold between proliferating and arrested populations, while stimulating lymphocytes to divide increased MELK expression 20-fold (Figure 5B–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 5B-C.

claim: Stimulating lymphocytes to divide increased MELK expression 20-fold.
source: Similarly, in human fibroblasts cultured until senescence, MELK expression decreased up to 11-fold between proliferating and arrested populations, while stimulating lymphocytes to divide increased MELK expression 20-fold (Figure 5B–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 5B-C.

claim: MELK levels reflect mitotic activity in diverse cell types.
source: These data suggest that MELK levels reflect mitotic activity in diverse cell types.
evidence: This conclusion is inferred from the correlation data presented.

claim: In cohorts of patients with breast cancer, glioma, or melanoma, MELK expression was significantly correlated with five proliferation markers (median correlation = 0.82).
source: In cohorts of patients with tumor types in which MELK levels have previously been associated with advanced disease, MELK expression was significantly correlated with each of the proliferation genes (median correlation = 0.82; Figure 5D).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 5D.

claim: MELK expression was significantly linked with poor outcome in 14 of 15 breast cancer datasets.
source: We found that MELK expression was significantly linked with poor outcome in 14 of 15 datasets (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by Cox proportional hazards analysis.

claim: A proliferation meta-gene was significantly associated with poor outcome in 13 of 15 breast cancer datasets.
source: Similarly, a proliferation meta-gene derived by averaging the normalized expression of MKI67, PCNA, CCNB1, MCM2, and TOP2A was significantly associated with poor outcome in 13 of 15 datasets (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by Cox proportional hazards analysis.

claim: The Z scores generated by univariate proliferation models were significantly correlated with the Z scores generated by univariate MELK models (R = 0.78, p<0.001).
source: Strikingly, we found that the Z scores generated by our univariate proliferation models were significantly correlated with the Z scores generated by the univariate MELK models: in patient cohorts in which proliferation was highly-prognostic, MELK expression was also highly-prognostic, and vice-versa (Figure 5E; R = 0.78, p<0.001).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 5E.

claim: MELK expression and cell proliferation capture very similar clinical information.
source: These analyses suggested that MELK expression and cell proliferation capture very similar clinical information.
evidence: This conclusion is inferred from the high correlation between MELK and proliferation Z scores.

claim: In bivariate models, MELK was significantly associated with patient outcome in only 2 of 15 breast cancer datasets.
source: In the bivariate models, MELK was significantly associated with patient outcome in only 2 of 15 datasets, demonstrating that considering tumor cell proliferation ablated MELK's clinical utility (Figure 5F).
evidence: This claim is supported by bivariate Cox proportional hazards analysis shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Considering tumor cell proliferation ablated MELK's clinical utility.
source: In the bivariate models, MELK was significantly associated with patient outcome in only 2 of 15 datasets, demonstrating that considering tumor cell proliferation ablated MELK's clinical utility (Figure 5F).
evidence: This conclusion is based on the bivariate analysis results.

claim: When tumors are stratified according to their proliferation level, MELK expression is no longer prognostic.
source: Thus, when tumors are stratified according to their proliferation level, MELK expression is no longer prognostic (Figure 5G).
evidence: This claim is supported by Kaplan-Meier analysis shown in Figure 5G.

claim: The observed pattern of MELK expression in cancer can be explained by the fact that MELK is up-regulated in mitotic cells.
source: In total, these results suggest that the observed pattern of MELK expression in cancer can be explained by the fact that MELK is up-regulated in mitotic cells.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the comprehensive gene expression and survival analyses.

claim: Combining CRISPR and a small-molecule inhibitor in a variety of assays failed to reveal a role for MELK in several cancer-related processes.
source: In this current manuscript, we report that combining CRISPR and a small-molecule inhibitor in a variety of assays failed to reveal a role for MELK in several cancer-related processes.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: Anti-MELK monotherapies are unlikely to be effective cancer treatments.
source: These results suggest that anti-MELK monotherapies are unlikely to be effective cancer treatments.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the comprehensive experimental data showing MELK is dispensable.

claim: Multiple cellular functions are dispensable for in vitro proliferation but required for tumor progression.
source: Nonetheless, multiple cellular functions are dispensable for in vitro proliferation but required for tumor progression, including stem cell renewal, oxygen sensing, and chemotherapy resistance (Rotem et al., 2015; Zhong et al., 2011; Miller et al., 2017; Cidado et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Several previous studies of MELK function may have been compromised by off-target activity of the constructs and inhibitors that were used.
source: We speculate that, as has previously been reported for one MELK inhibitor and one set of MELK-targeting shRNA's (Huang et al., 2017), several previous studies of MELK function may have been compromised by off-target activity of the constructs and inhibitors that were used.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for discrepancies with prior literature.

claim: Variability was observed between clones from the same parental cell line, and between clonal lines and the parental cell populations.
source: Of note, we observed variability between clones from the same parental cell line, and between clonal lines and the parental cell populations.
evidence: This observation is based on the experimental data presented.

claim: It is important to assess multiple independent clones and cell populations in CRISPR experiments.
source: These observations underscore the importance of assessing multiple independent clones and cell populations in CRISPR experiments.
evidence: This is a methodological recommendation based on the observed variability.

claim: 'Epistasis' experiments can be widely applied to assess the on-target consequences of acutely inhibiting potential cancer drug targets.
source: We suggest that these 'epistasis' experiments can be widely applied to assess the on-target consequences of acutely inhibiting potential cancer drug targets.
evidence: This is a methodological suggestion based on the approach used in this study.

claim: MELK transcript expression closely mirrors tumor mitotic activity.
source: As we observed no role for MELK as either an oncogene or a cancer dependency, we sought to instead investigate whether its cell cycle-dependent expression pattern could explain its prognostic value. Consistent with this hypothesis, we discovered that MELK transcript expression closely mirrors tumor mitotic activity.
evidence: This claim is supported by the gene expression correlation analyses presented.

claim: Actively-growing cancers appear to up-regulate thousands of genes involved in cell cycle progression when compared to quiescent normal tissue.
source: As actively-growing cancers appear to up-regulate thousands of genes involved in cell cycle progression when compared to quiescent normal tissue (Whitfield et al., 2006), this observation may explain why MELK is commonly over-expressed in different malignancies.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Rapid cell division in tumors is indicative of tissue de-differentiation and aggressive disease.
source: Moreover, rapid cell division in tumors is indicative of tissue de-differentiation and aggressive disease; therefore, most cell cycle-regulated genes are also associated with poor clinical outcome (Smith and Sheltzer, 2017; Venet et al., 2011; Gentles et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Most cell cycle-regulated genes are associated with poor clinical outcome.
source: Moreover, rapid cell division in tumors is indicative of tissue de-differentiation and aggressive disease; therefore, most cell cycle-regulated genes are also associated with poor clinical outcome (Smith and Sheltzer, 2017; Venet et al., 2011; Gentles et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Controlling for cell proliferation ablates the prognostic significance of MELK expression.
source: We further demonstrated that controlling for cell proliferation ablates the prognostic significance of MELK expression, suggesting that this link may explain its connection with outcome in cancer.
evidence: This claim is supported by the bivariate Cox analysis presented.

claim: Many cell cycle genes are suitable cancer drug targets (e.g. CDK4 and CDK6).
source: While many cell cycle genes are indeed suitable cancer drug targets (e.g. CDK4 and CDK6), other genes may be up-regulated during normal cell division but dispensable for this process (Venet et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge and a citation.

claim: Some genes may be up-regulated during normal cell division but dispensable for this process.
source: While many cell cycle genes are indeed suitable cancer drug targets (e.g. CDK4 and CDK6), other genes may be up-regulated during normal cell division but dispensable for this process (Venet et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: MELK is an example of a gene that is up-regulated during cell division but dispensable for this process.
source: We suggest that MELK is an example of the latter.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental findings.

claim: MELK-knockout mice display no observable deficiencies.
source: As MELK-knockout mice display no observable deficiencies, MELK's function may be redundant with other kinases (Wang et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: MELK's function may be redundant with other kinases.
source: As MELK-knockout mice display no observable deficiencies, MELK's function may be redundant with other kinases (Wang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the lack of phenotype in MELK-knockout mice.

claim: If MELK plays a role in cancer, it may be detectable only in very limited circumstances, and likely in vivo.
source: We believe that, if MELK does play a role in cancer, it may be detectable only in very limited circumstances, and likely in vivo.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential future findings.
